transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-05-03
Start: 11:00 AM PDT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jamal Reyes (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Alex Liu (Redwood CSM), Maya Chen (Verdant CTO), Tom Alvarez (Verdant SRE Lead), Lena Ortiz (Verdant PM)

Summary:
- Follow-up on Verdant production incident on 2027-04-30 that caused elevated latency and partial outages for inference endpoints.
- Discussed root cause analysis (RCA), short-term mitigations already applied, and longer-term reliability improvements and runbook updates.
- Agreed next steps: share final RCA, run dedicated benchmarks, update runbooks and schedule failure-mode runthrough.

Topics:
1) Incident timeline & RCA
2) Immediate mitigations already completed
3) Long-term reliability / architectural changes
4) Runbook/playbook and testing plan
5) Action items and owners

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Jamal: okay can we get started? Hey everyone thanks for hopping on. we wanted to run through the postmortem for the 4/30 incident and make sure the mitigations we've put in place look good to you and that we have clear next steps.
[00:00:22] Maya: yeah thanks jamal, appreciate you. we got hit pretty hard on our side, user facing latencies spiked, some jobs timed out. we need to make sure this doesn't happen again.
[00:00:35] Priya: absolutely. quick preface — we did a triage the night of and again yesterday. short version, there was a request storm combined with an unfortunate cache eviction pattern in the KV cache plus an autoscaler mis-signal. those together pushed the serving nodes into high tail latency and the fallback logic wasn't kicking in correctly.
[00:01:05] Tom: to add, our telemetry showed slow token generation for a subset of long-context requests. we saw the queue depth jump and then some nodes OOMed which caused pods to restart.
[00:01:21] Jamal: yes that matches our traces. detail from the runtime side — during heavy concurrent long-context requests the prefix/K V cache had a thrashing behavior; the runtime was warming and evicting frequently because of a subtle memory leak in a kernel path triggered by a very specific tokenization pattern.
[00:01:50] Lena: when you say kernel path, do you mean a gpu kernel or like a runtime optimization in the infer engine?
[00:01:58] Priya: it's a runtime execution path — the attention kernel selection logic that chooses a quantized path. under certain token length distributions it was allocating temp buffers and not freeing them fast enough; after enough cycles the host memory grew and the OS killed the process on some nodes. add autoscaler hysteresis and the cluster didn't scale fast enough.
[00:02:25] Maya: okay that is... not great. what was the immediate mitigation you applied?
[00:02:31] Jamal: immediate mitigations we did during incident: 1) rolled back the kernel selection flag to the previous safe default across affected pools, 2) temporarily increased reserved capacity for Verdant's dedicated pool to absorb the QPS spike, 3) tweaked the autoscaler thresholds to be more aggressive for short term, 4) disabled a non-critical optimization that caused excessive memory churn.
[00:02:57] Tom: i saw the reserved capacity increase, that helped. the rollback to safe defaults stopped the OOMs within about 4 minutes.
[00:03:06] Priya: we also pushed a hotfix to the runtime to ensure buffers are reclaimed deterministically in that path — that's in staging and we're pushing to prod after a small canary tomorrow.
[00:03:18] Maya: good. question — how confident are you that the hotfix covers all tokenization edge cases? last time we had mis- tokenization behave oddly for some biomedical prompts.
[00:03:31] Priya: fair point. coverage is improved; we've added a targeted test suite that includes long biomedical sequences, very long tokens, and it's exercised against quantized kernels. but we want to run Verdant-specific prompts through the canary before fully rolling out.
[00:03:50] Jamal: that's one of the next steps — priya will run dedicated benchmarks using Verdant's sample prompt corpus and share results.
[00:03:58] Lena: on the topic of detection — can we have better alerting for memory churn vs just OOM? we only saw the OOMs after the user impact started.
[00:04:08] Alex: good point. we can add a memory growth alert for the agent pool and a high-queue-depth early-warning alert. we currently have queue depth but thresholds were conservative. we'll propose new SLI thresholds.
[00:04:23] Tom: also the fallback logic — our app expected the Redwood API to fail fast under saturation and return 503 so we could degrade gracefully. in this case requests were hanging and timing out at the client layer. can we make the client fail faster?
[00:04:38] Priya: yes so two prongs — server side we can add a circuit-breaker that short-circuits requests when latency > X and drop to a controlled 503 so clients can degrade. also the SDK can expose a lower client timeout for critical routes.
[00:04:55] Jamal: we suggested configuring an explicit model fallback (smaller model) for Verdant traffic as part of routing policy. that way if the preferred model is under load, requests can be routed to a cheaper lower-latency variant.
[00:05:08] Maya: what about data integrity / logs? we wanted full traces for investigation — i uploaded the sample trace bundle to the shared folder but our compliance team also wants audit logs around key rotation and who touched configs during the incident.
[00:05:20] Jamal: we'll share all the support ticket exports and the full trace links. Alex will include the config change audit log from the control plane and timestamps.
[00:05:31] Alex: noted, i'll attach the control plane audit + config diffs and the incident timeline to the RCA.
[00:05:40] Tom: can you show where the autoscaler hysteresis is? we think our cluster scale out happened too slowly relative to the burst.
[00:05:50] Priya: sure i'll summarize — our autoscaler is rate-limited to avoid flapping; we had a 120s cool-down which in this burst prevented quick scale outs. we recommended reducing cool-down to 30s for Verdant's pool and adding a manual emergency scale override option.
[00:06:10] Lena: is that safe? will reducing cool-down increase cost significantly?
[00:06:16] Jamal: it will increase transient cost but it's a tradeoff — we can keep a higher baseline reserved capacity and keep cool-down conservative, or drop cool-down and rely less on big reserved capacity. Verdant has committed to a reserved buffer so for now we've increased capacity and plan to tune autoscaler more aggressively with more targeted tests.
[00:06:36] Maya: i want both — a lower cool-down for emergencies and a runbook that flips on emergency reserved capacity. we need actionable steps we can run without Redwood ops in the middle.
[00:06:47] Priya: agreed, that's our runbook goal. we'll propose a one-click emergency mode for Verdant's pool (toggle in console + API) that increases both reserved and burst capacity.
[00:06:58] Jamal: moving to long-term mitigations — we propose: 1) the runtime fix and a staged rollout, 2) improved SLI/alerting for memory churn and queue depth, 3) circuit-breaker and model-fallback routing policy per route, 4) more robust canary testing using Verdant's real prompts, 5) runbook updates with emergency capacity toggle.
[00:07:24] Tom: for the canary testing, can you also run worst-case concurrency tests — like sustained 95th-percentile QPS for 30 minutes with warmup?
[00:07:34] Priya: yes we plan to run 30 minute stress tests at target QPS levels and include KV warmup and cache prepopulation in the harness. we'll share the harness and results.
[00:07:46] Maya: we also want the SLA discussion documented — the outage touched a small percentage of requests but had large customer impact. can we get a proposal for credits or enterprise SLA adjustments?
[00:07:58] Jamal: we'll include an SLA-impact appendix in the RCA and the account team will reach out on credits; we can propose a one-off credit and also discuss changes to the SLA for dedicated customers.
[00:08:10] Lena: last question — is there any vector here for secret/key exposure? we rotate keys but want to confirm KMS events were fine.
[00:08:18] Alex: i checked key rotation logs — no KMS failures tied to the incident. we'll include the KMS audit in the RCA bundle.
[00:08:27] Maya: ok good.
[00:08:33] Jamal: to recap next steps — jamal to send an initial RCA draft by 5/6, priya to run and share the dedicated-pool benchmark and the canary plan by 5/10, tom to share additional trace logs by 5/5, alex to attach control plane audit and config diffs. we will also schedule a runbook walkthrough week of 5/10. any additions?
[00:08:54] Tom: that covers it. please include a list of recommended SLI thresholds so we can align alerts.
[00:09:00] Priya: will do, plus we'll include example Prometheus alert snippets and recommended thresholds for queue depth and host memory growth.
[00:09:10] Maya: thank you all. please mark items on the ticket, we want a short exec note to our leadership once RCA is finalized.
[00:09:18] Jamal: understood. thanks everyone. we'll follow up in writing and set the runbook walkthrough.

[00:10:00] --call continued with technical clarifications (traces, log locations, minor crosstalk)--
[00:30:00] Priya: (clarifying) the kernel flag we rolled back was 'fast_quant_attention_v2' which under certain token shapes allocated extra scratch memory. toggling it off returned behavior to previous baseline. that's the short-term rollback.
[00:33:00] Tom: ok when you push the hotfix can you include a debug flag so we can capture allocation stacks if something similar happens again?
[00:33:25] Priya: yes we can add a debug trace mode that is low overhead until enabled.
[00:45:00] Alex: i'll open the support bundle and link to the RCA doc and audit logs after this call.
[00:46:00] Jamal: final — we'll schedule the runbook walkthrough for 5/11 at 11am PT unless you prefer otherwise.
[00:46:15] Maya: 5/11 works. thanks.

End of transcript.
